description: The crusader princes, the siege of Antioch, the capture of Jerusalem in 1099 and its brutal aftermath.
content_html:
The Crusade Army Assembles

The army that left for the Holy Land in the summer and autumn of 1096 was not a single unified force under one commander. It was a coalition of separate contingents, each under its own noble leader, united by the cross on their tunics and the goal of Jerusalem. The leaders included Godfrey de Bouillon, Duke of Lower Lorraine, his brother Baldwin; Bohemond of Taranto and his nephew Tancred from southern Italy; Raymond of Toulouse from France; and Robert of Normandy, son of William the Conqueror.

The crusade army arrived in Constantinople in stages between November 1096 and May 1097. Emperor Alexios Komnenos received each leader in turn, extracting from them an oath to return any former Byzantine territory they recovered. This promise would create serious tensions later in the campaign. In June 1097, the combined army besieged and captured Nicaea, returning it to Byzantine control. Then the great march south through Anatolia began.

Key Fact

The First Crusade had no single commander. Leadership was shared (and frequently disputed) among major nobles from France, Flanders, Lorraine and southern Italy. This lack of unified command both weakened the crusade’s coordination and preserved it from collapsing when any individual leader failed.

The Siege of Antioch, 1097–1098

Antioch was one of the great cities of the ancient world and a natural stronghold. Its walls ran for miles along steep hillsides, and it was garrisoned by a Turkish force under Yaghi-Siyan. The crusade army arrived in October 1097 and began a siege that would last eight months — one of the most gruelling episodes of the entire campaign.

The crusaders suffered enormously. They lacked the supplies to besiege a major city through winter. Famine killed thousands; desertion was a constant problem; foraging parties were ambushed by Seljuk relief forces. Yet the army held on. The breakthrough came not from military assault but from treachery. A Muslim garrison commander named Firouz agreed to allow Bohemond’s men to scale the walls on the night of 2–3 June 1098. The crusaders poured into the city and seized it, massacring much of the population.

Within days of seizing the city, the crusaders found themselves trapped inside it. A massive Seljuk relief army under Kerbogha of Mosul arrived and surrounded Antioch. With dwindling food and morale collapsing, a monk named Peter Bartholomew reported a vision: the Holy Lance — the lance that had pierced Christ’s side at the crucifixion — was buried in the Church of St Peter in Antioch. A relic was duly “discovered”.

The effect on morale was dramatic. On 28 June 1098, the crusader army, carrying the Holy Lance, marched out through Antioch’s gates and attacked Kerbogha’s far larger force. Kerbogha’s coalition proved fragile: individual Muslim commanders had their own rivalries and withdrew. The crusaders won a decisive victory. Whether the Holy Lance was genuine was disputed even at the time — a papal legate tested it by ordeal — but its psychological impact was real and measurable.

The March to Jerusalem and the Siege, 1099

After Antioch the crusade army was depleted, fractured by disputes over who would control Antioch (Bohemond seized it for himself, violating his oath to Alexios), and weakened by disease. Yet the goal of Jerusalem sustained the march south. The army arrived before Jerusalem on 7 June 1099. The city was defended by a Fatimid Egyptian garrison that had expelled the Seljuks the previous year.

The crusaders had no siege equipment. A first assault on 13 June failed. A period of desperate hardship followed — the summer heat was intense, and the area around Jerusalem had little water. Morale was at crisis point when a fleet arrived at Jaffa carrying timber and craftsmen. By mid-July the crusaders had built two great siege towers. On the night of 13–14 July 1099, they launched a coordinated assault. On 15 July 1099, Godfrey de Bouillon’s men breached the north wall and the city fell.

Key Fact

Jerusalem fell on 15 July 1099, after a campaign lasting nearly three years. Godfrey de Bouillon entered the city but refused the title of King, accepting instead the title “Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre”. He died the following year, in July 1100, and was succeeded by his brother Baldwin I, who took the title of King.

The capture of Jerusalem was followed by a massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. Contemporary sources — both crusader and Muslim — describe widespread killing in the streets and in the mosques and synagogues where people had taken refuge. The scale described in crusader sources may be exaggerated for dramatic and spiritual effect, but that a significant massacre occurred is not in doubt. The Jewish community, which had fled to a synagogue, was killed or sold into slavery.

The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem was now established. The results of the First Crusade were enormous. After years of hardship, starvation, disease and combat, a small army of Western knights had achieved what contemporaries regarded as a miracle — the liberation of the holiest city in Christendom. The Christian West had demonstrated that it could project military power deep into the eastern Mediterranean. But maintaining the new kingdom would prove a constant and draining challenge.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the First Crusade often focus on either the siege of Antioch or the fall of Jerusalem. For 8-mark questions, don’t just describe what happened — explain why it happened and what made it significant. For example, explain how the Holy Lance showed the importance of morale and religious belief in military outcomes, rather than just describing its discovery. For source questions, think about who wrote the source, why they wrote it, and what their perspective limits or enriches.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First Crusade army was a coalition of separate noble contingents with no single commander; after Nicaea it marched south to Antioch, which fell in June 1098 through treachery rather than assault.
  • The discovery of the Holy Lance at Antioch restored crusader morale and contributed to the victory over Kerbogha’s relief army on 28 June 1098.
  • Jerusalem fell on 15 July 1099 after a siege using timber siege towers; the capture was followed by a massacre of the Muslim and Jewish populations, and the establishment of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Siege of Antioch (1097–1098).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students may describe: the siege lasted eight months; the crusaders suffered from famine and disease; it ended when a garrison commander (Firouz) allowed Bohemond's men to scale the walls; a Seljuk relief army under Kerbogha then trapped the crusaders inside the city. 1 mark for a simple point; 2 marks for a developed point with supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the capture of Jerusalem in 1099.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should identify two features with supporting detail.
Feature 1: Jerusalem was captured on 15 July 1099 after the crusaders built timber siege towers that allowed them to breach the north wall; this followed a period of extreme hardship including intense summer heat and lack of water.
Feature 2: The capture was followed by a massacre of the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants; Godfrey de Bouillon entered the city but refused the title of King, taking instead the title 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre'.
2 marks per feature: 1 mark for simple point, 2 marks for developed point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the crusaders were able to capture Antioch in June 1098.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific reason (treachery of Firouz; the role of Bohemond; the failure of earlier assaults making the infiltration necessary) and explains it with precise detail, linking cause to outcome. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a reason with explanation and some link to outcome.
Developing: Identifies a reason but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Holy Lance for the outcome of the First Crusade.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Significance at the time — the discovery restored morale when the crusade was on the verge of collapse inside Antioch; it contributed to the victory over Kerbogha's army on 28 June 1098. Over time — it became a symbol of divine support for the crusade; debates over its authenticity reflected wider questions about the nature of crusading motivation and the role of religious belief. Sustained judgement.
Secure: Covers both dimensions with evidence; clear explanation.
Developing: Mainly describes the discovery with limited significance analysis.
Emerging: Describes the Holy Lance with little sense of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of Jerusalem in 1099.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (establishment of the Latin Kingdom; massacre of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants; the crusade became the model for all future crusades; fundamentally altered Christian-Muslim relations in the eastern Mediterranean) and explains it with precise detail. Sustained reasoning.
Secure: Identifies a consequence with some explanation.
Developing: Identifies a consequence but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.

practice_questions.text: 'The lack of a single commander was the main reason the First Crusade nearly failed.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues in support (disputes over Antioch almost broke the crusade; Bohemond's refusal to honour his oath damaged relations with Byzantium; lack of unified supply chain caused famine) and against (the coalition structure allowed the crusade to survive individual failures; religious motivation and the indulgence compensated for poor organisation; the Holy Lance incident showed morale could be rescued). Substantiated judgement.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence; conclusion reached.
Developing: Mainly one-sided, limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.

knowledge_checks.q: Who was the first ruler of Jerusalem after its capture in 1099?
How did the crusaders finally enter Antioch on the night of 2–3 June 1098?
options: They broke through the main city gate after a prolonged assault
A garrison commander named Firouz allowed them to scale the walls
They bribed the entire garrison to surrender

knowledge_checks.q: Jerusalem fell to the crusaders on 15 July _____.
The _____ was a relic discovered at Antioch that restored crusader morale before the battle against Kerbogha.
Match each crusade leader with their region of origin.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Siege of Antioch begin?
How did the crusaders enter Antioch in June 1098?
flashcard_questions.a: Through the treachery of a garrison commander named Firouz.

flashcard_questions.q: Who commanded the Seljuk relief army that trapped the crusaders inside Antioch?
What relic was 'discovered' at Antioch in June 1098?
flashcard_questions.a: The Holy Lance, supposedly the lance that pierced Christ at the crucifixion.

flashcard_questions.q: On what date did Jerusalem fall to the crusaders?
Who entered Jerusalem first and what title did he refuse?
flashcard_questions.a: Godfrey de Bouillon; he refused the title of King.

flashcard_questions.q: What title did Godfrey de Bouillon accept in Jerusalem instead of King?
What crusader state was established after the capture of Jerusalem?
What oath did the crusade leaders swear to Alexios Komnenos before leaving Constantinople?
flashcard_questions.a: To return any former Byzantine territory they recovered to Byzantium.

flashcard_questions.q: Which crusade leader broke his oath to Alexios by keeping Antioch?
The crusader army captured Nicaea in which year?
What material did a supply fleet bring to Jerusalem in July 1099 that enabled the final assault?
flashcard_questions.a: Timber, used to build siege towers.

glossary_terms.definition: A French noble (c.1060–1100) who led the Lotharingian contingent on the First Crusade and became the first ruler of Jerusalem, taking the title 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre'.
A relic supposedly discovered at Antioch in June 1098, believed to be the lance that pierced Christ's side at the crucifixion; its discovery significantly restored crusader morale.
The crusader state established after the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, ruled initially by Godfrey de Bouillon and then by the Kings of Jerusalem.

hero_image_caption: Crusader forces besieging Jerusalem in July 1099, capturing it on the 15th of that month.
